summary:
Ondo State stands under Nigeria's national framework. Same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across the country since 1916, and the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, criminalises all forms of same-sex unions with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

The death-penalty layer does not reach Ondo. The twelve states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes, where male sodomy can be punished by death including by stoning, sit in the northern part of the country; Ondo, a southern state, stands under the secular framework, where the maximum penalty recorded is a life sentence.

The southern states, Ondo included, also operate a separate gross-indecency offence under Section 217 of the Criminal Code: any male committing or procuring an act of gross indecency with another male, in public or private, is guilty of a felony liable to three years' imprisonment. Victor Oluwasina Ayeni, senior lecturer in law at Adekunle Ajasin University in Ondo state, observed in a January 2017 book chapter that the Code fails to define what constitutes an act of gross indecency, leaving the offence's scope open to discretionary application.

Nigeria records no legal recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protections and no recognition of same-sex relationships. The UK Home Office's June 2025 country policy and information note documents countrywide harm patterns of arrests, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people under this framework.

Trans Nigerians face lethal violence with official misgendering and subsequent impunity. The beaten body of the Abuja trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender woman, was found on the Katampe-Mabushi expressway in Abuja on 9 August 2024; police opened a 'thorough and discreet' investigation.

No state-specific protective statute or enforcement divergence is documented for Ondo; the national framework, including the gross-indecency offence applicable in southern states such as Ondo, applies without recorded variation.
tangentialFactors:
Countrywide, mass arrests of LGBTQ+ Nigerians are common, especially in northern states, and the UK Home Office records arrests, detention and mob violence as harm patterns applying across all states including Ondo.

Ondo is not named in Wikipedia's Nigeria LGBT-rights overview, so the state-specific picture rests on inference from its status as a southern state under the secular framework rather than on documented incidents within its borders.
localsOnly:
Adekunle Ajasin University in Ondo state employs Victor Oluwasina Ayeni as a senior lecturer in law; his January 2017 book chapter critiquing the Criminal Code's undefined 'gross indecency' standard is the only Ondo-specific scholarly contribution recorded in the inventory.

Residents of Ondo face the same three-year felony exposure under Criminal Code Section 217 and the 14-year SSMPA penalty as other southerners, with no state-level protection on gender identity, discrimination or relationship recognition.
outOfScopeNotes:
Ondo is not named in the Wikipedia overview or the UK Home Office note as a site of specific arrests, incidents or enforcement actions; the absence of state-specific records is unresolved rather than evidence of non-enforcement.

No Ondo-specific data on policing practice, venue closures, dating-app entrapment or healthcare access for LGBT+ people appears in the inventory; whether national patterns documented elsewhere in Nigeria occur inside Ondo is not sourced here.

The inventory contains no information on document or marker rules, entry screening, facilities access or partner recognition as they apply to a trans visitor specifically at Ondo's borders or within the state.
